notes: One durable outbox entry per purchase, keyed by the store transaction id (Google Play: the purchase token).
An entry records, when its send is admitted: signedTransaction, reason, requesterDistinctId and customerKind. Every retry sends exactly these; it never works them out again.

reason is 'purchase' for the customer's own checkout (including a store delivery of a checkout still running, and the product the store says they already own, for that product only), 'restore' for Restore, and 'sync' for every other send: store updates, launch recovery, deferred approvals, and the scans after identify or reset.

customerKind is 'identified' when the requester signed in with identify and 'anonymous' when they did not. When the SDK cannot tell (a requester no longer on the device when their entry is admitted) it is 'identified': the server merges only owners declared anonymous, so such a customer can be moved but never merged away.

requesterDistinctId is the customer the send is for: the one an explicit producer (checkout, Restore, already owned) names, else the customer of the checkout binding the store delivery matches, else the current customer. A scan with no purpose names no one: its current customer is only that last fallback, so it never outranks a binding. A checkout binding is matched only by a purchase the store did not already own when that checkout began, so a completion only ever comes from the checkout's own new purchase. A checkout's $purchase_completed is captured only while its buyer is the current customer (the event log stamps the current identity on every event and routes it to the current customer's Journeys); until then it waits on the buyer's saved entry, which retires the binding once it holds the completion, or, while the outbox is off, in the binding, which is retired only when the completion is captured. The SDK never works out who owns a purchase; the owner is what the server last said.

A 200 or a refusal (409, 400) answers the send and clears the entry. Any other failure (transport, 5xx, 401, 403) keeps it with one more attempt and records when it is due again: the failure time plus the delay for its attempt count. The attempt count and due time survive restarts. One outbox timer is set to the earliest due time of the entries still waiting, or to now when one is already due, after every send result (accepted, refused or failed) and at launch, and is cancelled when none is waiting; when it fires it sends every entry whose due time has passed, and a due entry it tries but cannot send counts one more failed attempt. A timer pass sends only entries that are due; the store's unfinished-purchase scan runs at launch, identify, reset, catalog change and Restore, never from the timer. Every unsent entry is also sent at every launch, at identify or reset, and when a newly loaded profile changes the product catalog. When the outbox cannot save (an entry, checkout binding or catalog-mapping write fails, or a store cannot be read right now), it is off for the rest of the session: nothing unlocks early, the timer is cancelled and stays off, and nothing is held in memory. Each purchase the store delivers (the checkout's result, a store update, a scan, Restore) is still sent once, its answer only refreshes the profile (no $purchase_synced, no 200 Features), and its transaction is never finished, so the next launch saves its entry, sends it and finishes it as normal. This holds whichever write of a commit fails, also one after its entry was first saved (its finish or delivered completion): the purchase is still sent once and its completion captured in the session. A store delivery of a purchase whose entry on disk is already answered is not sent again, because that entry is still its record; a Restore's or an already-owned claim is always sent once. Stored entries the store does not deliver wait for the next launch, and a failed binding or catalog-mapping write does not fail the checkout, which carries on with its in-memory context.

Every write that changes what an entry sends (signedTransaction, requesterDistinctId, reason, customerKind, or a refund's signed revocation), or opens an answered entry again, is an admission with a fresh admissionId; bookkeeping writes keep it. Each send carries its entry's admissionId, and its answer clears, answers or counts a failed attempt on the entry only while the entry still holds that admissionId; otherwise it only triggers the profile refresh. Changes to one purchase run one at a time: while an answer is applied (admission check, entry change, Feature publication and 200 hold together), a new admission for that purchase waits until it has finished. Every write to an entry checks the admission it was based on against the current entry in the same step, and is dropped when that admission is gone; only the store's finish of the transaction and its captured checkout completion are recorded on whichever entry holds it. Nothing an answer gives is published before the answer is saved, so one that cannot be saved publishes nothing. A write or send built from an earlier store read never downgrades the entry: once the entry holds the purchase's signed revocation, a claim or send from a read that saw the purchase active is dropped (a Restore does not count it, as a fresh read leaves a refunded purchase out), and the entry keeps the revocation as its next send.

Every answer, from a scan's send, the outbox pass, a Restore or purchase claim, or a purchase-backed Feature command, passes one admission check before it may change its entry or a 200 hold. A purchase-backed Feature command writes its post-use result in that same step and lets go of the purchase only after it, so a Restore waiting on the purchase admits its claim afterwards. A superseded answer (its admission is no longer the entry's) only refreshes the profile: from any producer, including a purchase-backed Feature command whose caller still gets its result, it changes no Feature authority, cache, entry or hold. No session cache decides sending, clearing or access: an answered entry stays as the purchase's record (finished, completion delivered) until it expires, and a later delivery of the purchase reads its flags instead of sending again.

After any answer, accepted or refused, the SDK fetches the requester's profile again when they are the current customer. Access comes only from the server profile, plus the early unlock of the buyer's own unanswered, unrevoked purchase (its account token is the one derived for the current customer). While the outbox is off there is no early unlock, and a purchase-backed Feature use takes the ordinary Feature command. A 200's features hold in memory only until a profile requested after them lands. Retiring that hold counts as a change to each Feature, so a Feature check that began before it cannot publish over the profile. Such a check is discarded and asked again, so its caller gets the current answer. This holds for every Feature the check would write: the one it asked about and the answer's balance source (a credit wallet, say).

Restore sends every current store entitlement for the restoring customer as 'restore' and reports restored only when the server accepted at least one. It reports owned by another account only when every claim was refused, and unconfirmed when none was accepted and at least one is unanswered, even if others were refused. Each claim is written into the outbox as the restoring customer's entry before it is sent, so an unanswered claim is retried like any other entry. With one entry per purchase, a claim takes over another customer's entry for the same purchase. A Restore claim never unlocks before the server answers. Each explicit Restore is a new admission (fresh admissionId, attempts and due time reset) and sends its own claim, even when a queued claim has the same fields; only that send's answer counts for it.

Android has no client refund signal: its early unlock is the buyer's own unanswered entry, sent until the server answers, so a refund or cancellation before that answer keeps the early unlock until it arrives (seconds online, or until back online), the same class as the accepted offline case. iOS keeps StoreKit's signed revocation as a fact on the entry, which stops the early unlock at once.

Entries in a previous SDK's format, recognised by having no admissionId, are dropped when the outbox is read: pre-GA local state with no compatibility handling. The store redelivers unfinished purchases, which then go through the outbox normally. A store file whose bytes are read but do not decode (invalid JSON, or a current-format entry that cannot be read) is corrupt: it is renamed aside as <name>.unreadable-<epoch millis>.json, never read again, and an empty store takes its place with the outbox on (only the newest quarantined file per store is kept, and each quarantine is logged once by entry and field, never values), while a store that cannot be read right now (a read error, no bytes read) is left as it is and keeps the outbox off for the session.
Runners drive production entry points (checkout, already-owned checkout, Restore, store update, launch scan, stored retry) against a transport that records each request and answers as the case says.

sends.name: the product the store says is already owned
a retry after reset keeps the recorded fields
